q: Positive rays (canal rays) were discovered in 1886 by:
x: Goldstein used a discharge tube with a perforated cathode and saw rays passing through the holes behind it. Thomson studied cathode rays (electrons) and Chadwick discovered the neutron.

q: In Goldstein's discharge tube with a perforated cathode, the positive rays were observed:
o: Behind the cathode, after passing through its holes
Behind the anode, moving away from the cathode
Only at the surface of the anode
Only when a magnetic field was applied
x: Positive ions formed in the gas move towards the negative cathode; some pass through its holes and appear as a glow behind it. That is why they are also called canal rays.

q: The e/m value of positive rays is highest when the discharge tube contains:
x: The H⁺ ion (a proton) is the lightest positive ion, so for the same charge it has the largest e/m. Heavier gases give heavier ions and smaller e/m values.

q: Which statement correctly contrasts positive rays with cathode rays?
o: Both have the same e/m whatever gas is used
Positive rays are much lighter than cathode ray particles
The e/m of positive rays depends on the gas in the tube; that of cathode rays does not
Cathode rays are deflected by fields but positive rays are not
x: Cathode rays are always electrons, so their e/m is constant. Positive rays are ions of whatever gas is present, so their mass and e/m change with the gas.

q: Positive rays are produced in a discharge tube when:
o: Protons are emitted directly from the anode metal
Cathode ray electrons knock electrons out of gas molecules
Neutrons in the gas gain a positive charge
Electrons combine with gas molecules to form ions
x: Fast cathode rays collide with gas molecules and remove electrons, leaving positive ions; these ions form the positive rays. Gaining electrons would give negative ions, not positive rays.

q: The mass of a proton is approximately:
x: A proton has a mass of 1.6726 × 10⁻²⁷ kg (1.6726 × 10⁻²⁴ g). 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg is the electron's mass and 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ is the size of the charge in coulombs.

q: Compared with an electron, a proton is:
x: The proton mass (1.6726 × 10⁻²⁷ kg) divided by the electron mass (9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg) is about 1836.

q: Which statement about the proton is correct?
o: Its mass is nearly equal to that of an electron
Its charge is equal in size but opposite in sign to an electron's charge
Its e/m value is greater than that of an electron
x: A proton carries +1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, the same size as the electron's −1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. Because it is about 1836 times heavier, its e/m is much smaller than the electron's.

q: Which statement about positive rays is NOT correct?
o: They are deflected by electric and magnetic fields
Their e/m depends on the gas in the tube
Their particles have the same mass whatever gas is used
x: Positive rays are ions of the gas in the tube, so their mass changes with the gas; this is why their e/m varies. The other three statements are true properties of positive rays.

q: When hydrogen gas is used in a discharge tube, the positive rays consist of:
x: Removing the single electron from a hydrogen atom leaves H⁺, which is a proton. This is how the proton was identified as the lightest positive particle.

q: According to Planck's quantum theory, energy is emitted or absorbed:
o: Only by gases at high temperature
Discontinuously, in small packets called quanta
x: Planck proposed that radiant energy is emitted or absorbed in separate packets (quanta), not continuously. A quantum of light is called a photon.

q: In the equation E = hν, the value of Planck's constant h is:
x: h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s. 6.022 × 10²³ is Avogadro's number, 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ is the electronic charge in coulombs and 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ is the electron's mass in kg.

q: The energy of a photon is directly proportional to its:
x: E = hν, so energy rises in direct proportion to frequency. Since E = hc/λ, energy is inversely, not directly, proportional to wavelength.

q: If the wavelength of a radiation is doubled, the energy of each of its photons becomes:
x: E = hc/λ, so energy is inversely proportional to wavelength. Doubling λ halves the energy of each photon.

q: Which of these radiations has photons of the highest energy?
x: X-rays have the highest frequency (shortest wavelength) of the four, and E = hν. Infrared has the lowest frequency, so the least energy per photon.

q: A radiation has a frequency of 5 × 10¹⁴ Hz. Taking h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, the energy of one photon is:
x: E = hν = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ × 5 × 10¹⁴ = 33 × 10⁻²⁰ = 3.3 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Dividing h by ν instead of multiplying gives 1.32 × 10⁻⁴⁸ J.

q: Taking h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, the energy of a photon of wavelength 300 nm is:
x: E = hc/λ = (6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3 × 10⁸)/(3 × 10⁻⁷ m) = 6.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Leaving λ as 300 instead of converting nm to m gives 6.6 × 10⁻²⁸ J.

q: The wave number of a radiation is:
o: The number of waves passing a point per second
The product of frequency and wavelength
x: Wave number = 1/λ, the number of waves per unit length (e.g. m⁻¹). Waves passing per second is the frequency, and the distance between crests is the wavelength.

q: The term photon refers to:
o: A positively charged particle in the nucleus
x: A photon is one quantum of electromagnetic radiation, carrying energy hν. It is not a charged particle.

q: Two radiations have wavelengths of 200 nm and 400 nm. The ratio of the energy of a photon of the first to that of the second is:
x: E = hc/λ, so E₁/E₂ = λ₂/λ₁ = 400/200 = 2. The shorter wavelength carries twice the energy per photon.

q: According to Bohr's theory, an electron in a hydrogen atom emits energy when it:
o: Jumps from a higher orbit to a lower orbit
Jumps from a lower orbit to a higher orbit
x: Bohr said an electron does not radiate while in a fixed orbit. It emits a photon when it falls to a lower orbit and absorbs energy when it moves to a higher one.

q: Bohr's condition for an allowed orbit is that the angular momentum of the electron, mvr, equals:
x: Bohr postulated that angular momentum is quantised: mvr = nh/2π, where n = 1, 2, 3 … Only orbits that meet this condition are allowed.

q: The Lyman series of the hydrogen spectrum lies in the:
x: Lyman lines come from electrons falling to n = 1; these are large energy gaps, so the lines are in the ultraviolet. The Balmer series (to n = 2) is the visible one.

q: An electron falls from an orbit of energy E₂ to a lower orbit of energy E₁. The frequency of the emitted radiation is:
x: The energy given out equals the difference between the orbits: ΔE = E₂ − E₁ = hν, so ν = (E₂ − E₁)/h.

q: In a hydrogen atom, an electron falls from n = 5 to n = 3. The line produced belongs to the:
x: The series is named by the lower (final) level: n = 1 Lyman, n = 2 Balmer, n = 3 Paschen, n = 4 Brackett. A fall to n = 3 gives a Paschen line in the infrared.

q: In Bohr's model the energy of the electron in the first orbit of hydrogen is E₁. Its energy in the third orbit is:
x: Eₙ is proportional to 1/n², so E₃ = E₁/3² = E₁/9. Since E₁ is negative, E₃ is less negative, i.e. higher in energy.

q: The radius of the first Bohr orbit of hydrogen is 0.529 Å. The radius of the second orbit is:
x: The radius is proportional to n², so r₂ = 0.529 × 2² = 2.116 Å. Multiplying by n instead of n² gives the wrong value 1.058 Å; 4.761 Å is the third orbit.

q: According to Bohr's model, as n increases, the energy difference between successive orbits of hydrogen:
x: Energy depends on 1/n², so the levels crowd closer together as n increases. The gap between n = 1 and 2 is much larger than between n = 4 and 5.

q: The spectrum of hydrogen is a line spectrum and not a continuous one because:
o: The electron can have only certain fixed energies
The electron radiates energy continuously as it orbits
The nucleus itself emits the light
x: Energy levels in the atom are quantised, so only certain energy differences, and hence certain frequencies, are possible. Each allowed jump gives one sharp line.

q: Which electron transition in a hydrogen atom produces a line of the Balmer series?
x: Balmer lines are emitted when electrons fall to n = 2 from higher levels. A fall to n = 1 is Lyman, to n = 3 is Paschen, and n = 2 to n = 4 is absorption, not emission.

q: Bohr's model successfully explained the spectrum of:
o: The hydrogen atom and one-electron species
x: Bohr's model works for hydrogen and other species with only one electron (such as He⁺). It fails for atoms with more than one electron.

q: An atomic orbital is best described as:
o: A fixed circular path of an electron around the nucleus
The total number of electrons in a shell
The region of space around the nucleus where the probability of finding an electron is maximum
The path followed by a photon
x: An orbital is a three-dimensional region of high electron probability. A fixed circular path is Bohr's orbit, an older idea.

q: The maximum number of electrons that one atomic orbital can hold is:
x: Each orbital holds at most two electrons, and they must have opposite spins (Pauli exclusion principle). Eight is the maximum for the second shell, not an orbital.

q: Which statement correctly distinguishes an orbit from an orbital?
o: An orbit is a definite circular path; an orbital is a region of probability
An orbit holds two electrons; an orbital holds 2n² electrons
An orbital is a definite circular path; an orbit is a region of probability
They are two names for the same thing
x: Bohr's orbit is a fixed planar path at a fixed distance. An orbital, from wave mechanics, is a 3-D region where the electron is likely to be found.

q: The idea of a definite electron path was replaced by the orbital concept mainly because:
o: The exact position and momentum of an electron cannot both be known at the same time
Electrons always move in straight lines
The nucleus is too small to be measured
x: Heisenberg's uncertainty principle shows we cannot fix both the position and the momentum of an electron, so only the probability of finding it can be described. That probability region is the orbital.

q: Orbitals of the same subshell that have equal energy, such as the three 2p orbitals, are called:
x: Orbitals of equal energy are degenerate. In a free atom the three p orbitals of a subshell are degenerate, as are the five d orbitals.

q: An atomic orbital is completely identified by which set of quantum numbers?
x: n gives the shell, l the subshell (shape) and m the orientation, so these three fix one orbital. The spin quantum number s identifies an electron within the orbital, not the orbital itself.

q: In an electron-cloud (dot) picture of an orbital, the dots are most crowded where:
o: The nucleus is located in every case
No electron can ever be found
The probability of finding the electron is greatest
x: The density of dots shows the probability of finding the electron: more dots, greater probability. For a p orbital, the dots are absent at the nucleus.

q: The total number of atomic orbitals in the fourth shell (n = 4) is:
x: The number of orbitals in a shell is n², so n = 4 has 16 orbitals (one 4s, three 4p, five 4d, seven 4f). 32 is the maximum number of electrons (2n²).

q: Which orbital designation is NOT possible?
x: For n = 2, l can only be 0 or 1, giving 2s and 2p. A d subshell needs l = 2, which first appears at n = 3.

q: The three orbitals of a 2p subshell differ from one another in their:
x: px, py and pz have the same shape, size and energy in a free atom; they point along different axes. Orientation is given by the magnetic quantum number m.

q: The principal quantum number (n) of an electron tells us its:
o: Main shell, which decides its energy and the size of the orbital
x: n gives the main energy level (shell): higher n means higher energy and a larger orbital. Shape is given by l, orientation by m and spin by s.

q: The azimuthal quantum number (l) for a d subshell is:
x: l = 0, 1, 2, 3 correspond to s, p, d, f subshells. So a d subshell has l = 2.

q: For the third shell (n = 3), the allowed values of the azimuthal quantum number l are:
x: l takes values from 0 to n − 1. For n = 3, l = 0, 1, 2, giving the 3s, 3p and 3d subshells.

q: For an electron with l = 2, the number of possible values of the magnetic quantum number m is:
x: m runs from −l to +l: −2, −1, 0, +1, +2, which is 5 values. This is why a d subshell has five orbitals.

q: The maximum number of electrons that can be accommodated in the third shell (n = 3) is:
x: The maximum is 2n² = 2 × 3² = 18. Nine is the number of orbitals (n²) in this shell.

q: The maximum number of electrons that an f subshell can hold is:
x: An f subshell (l = 3) has 2l + 1 = 7 orbitals, and each holds two electrons, giving 14. Seven is the number of orbitals, not electrons.

q: Which set of quantum numbers (n, l, m, s) is NOT allowed?
x: l must be less than n, so n = 2 cannot have l = 2. The other sets obey all the rules: l from 0 to n − 1, m from −l to +l, and s = ±½.

q: The spin quantum number (s) of an electron can have the values:
x: An electron spins either clockwise or anticlockwise, given by s = +½ or −½. Whole numbers from −l to +l are the values of m.

q: The maximum number of electrons in an atom that can have n = 3 and l = 1 is:
x: n = 3, l = 1 is the 3p subshell, with three orbitals (m = −1, 0, +1). Each holds two electrons, so 6 electrons.

q: Which quantum number mainly determines the shape of an orbital?
x: l decides the subshell and so the shape: l = 0 spherical s, l = 1 dumbbell p. n decides size and energy, and m the orientation.

q: The shape of an s orbital is:
x: An s orbital is spherically symmetrical around the nucleus. p orbitals are dumbbell shaped.

q: The shape of a p orbital is:
x: A p orbital has two lobes on opposite sides of the nucleus, giving a dumbbell shape. s orbitals are spherical.

q: The number of nodal planes in a single p orbital is:
x: Each p orbital has one nodal plane passing through the nucleus, which separates its two lobes. An s orbital has no nodal plane.

q: A px orbital has its lobes along the x-axis. Its nodal plane is the:
x: The nodal plane is perpendicular to the axis of the lobes and passes through the nucleus. For px, that is the yz plane.

q: As the principal quantum number increases from 1s to 2s to 3s, the s orbital:
x: All s orbitals are spherical; a higher n gives a larger orbital with the electron on average farther from the nucleus.

q: Which of these orbitals is non-directional, i.e. the same in all directions from the nucleus?
x: An s orbital is spherically symmetrical, so it has no preferred direction. Each p orbital is concentrated along one axis.

q: Which statement about the three 2p orbitals of a free atom is correct?
o: They all lie along the same axis
They differ in energy and in shape
They are perpendicular to one another and equal in energy
x: px, py and pz point along the three axes at 90° to each other and are degenerate in a free atom. They are dumbbell shaped, not spherical.

q: Compared with a 1s orbital, a 2s orbital is:
o: The same size but dumbbell shaped
Larger, with one spherical node inside it
x: A 2s orbital is spherical like 1s but larger, and it has one spherical node (a shell of zero probability) between the inner and outer regions. Nodal planes belong to p orbitals.

q: The probability of finding an electron of a p orbital exactly at the nucleus is:
o: The same as for an s orbital
x: The nucleus lies on the nodal plane of every p orbital, where the probability of finding the electron is zero. s orbitals, by contrast, have a high probability near the nucleus.

q: Which statement about a p orbital is correct?
o: It has a single lobe centred on the nucleus
It has four lobes in one plane
It has the same shape as an s orbital
It has two lobes on opposite sides of the nucleus
x: A p orbital has two lobes, one on each side of the nucleus, along one axis. Four lobes in a plane describe most d orbitals.

q: The Aufbau principle states that electrons:
o: Must have opposite spins in every orbital
Fill orbitals in order of increasing energy
Fill orbitals in order of decreasing energy
x: Aufbau ('building up') means electrons enter the lowest-energy orbital available first. Opposite spins is Pauli's principle and filling degenerate orbitals singly is Hund's rule.

q: The Pauli exclusion principle states that:
o: Electrons fill the lowest energy orbitals first
Electrons pair up only after all degenerate orbitals have one electron
The position and momentum of an electron cannot both be known
No two electrons in an atom can have the same set of four quantum numbers
x: Pauli's principle means two electrons in the same orbital must differ in spin. The other statements are the Aufbau principle, Hund's rule and the uncertainty principle.

q: Hund's rule states that electrons entering degenerate orbitals:
o: Pair up in the first orbital before the next is used
Always have opposite spins in separate orbitals
Enter the orbital of highest energy first
Occupy them singly with parallel spins before pairing begins
x: Electrons spread out one per orbital, with parallel spins, before any pairing occurs; this gives the most unpaired electrons and lower energy.

q: The 4s subshell is filled before the 3d subshell because:
o: 4s has a lower (n + l) value than 3d
4s has a higher principal quantum number
4s is closer to the nucleus than 3d
x: For 4s, n + l = 4 + 0 = 4; for 3d, n + l = 3 + 2 = 5. The subshell with the lower n + l has lower energy and fills first.

q: According to the (n + l) rule, when two subshells have the same (n + l) value, the one filled first is the one with the:
x: With equal n + l, the subshell with lower n has lower energy. For example 3d and 4p both have n + l = 5, and 3d fills first.

q: A student writes the 2p electrons of nitrogen as one paired orbital (↑↓), one orbital with ↑ and one empty orbital. This arrangement breaks:
x: Nitrogen's three 2p electrons should occupy the three 2p orbitals singly with parallel spins (↑ ↑ ↑). Pairing while an orbital of equal energy is empty breaks Hund's rule.

q: An orbital containing two electrons with the same spin (↑↑) breaks:
x: Two electrons in one orbital already share n, l and m, so they must differ in spin. Two parallel spins in one orbital would give identical sets of four quantum numbers.

q: Which is the correct order of filling of subshells?
x: By the (n + l) rule, 4s (4) fills before 3d (5), and 3d fills before 4p (also 5) because it has the lower n.

q: According to Hund's rule, the number of unpaired electrons in an oxygen atom (Z = 8) is:
x: Oxygen is 1s² 2s² 2p⁴. The four 2p electrons go ↑↓, ↑, ↑ in the three 2p orbitals, leaving two unpaired electrons.

q: According to the (n + l) rule, which of these subshells has the highest energy?
x: n + l values: 4s = 4, 3d = 5, 4p = 5, 5s = 5. Among those with 5, the one with the highest n (5s) has the highest energy, so the order is 4s < 3d < 4p < 5s.

q: The electronic configuration of sodium (Z = 11) is:
x: Eleven electrons fill 1s², 2s², 2p⁶ and then one electron enters 3s. A p subshell cannot hold seven electrons, and 3s fills before 3p.

q: The electronic configuration of chromium (Z = 24) is:
x: Chromium is an exception: one 4s electron moves into 3d to give the more stable half-filled 3d⁵, so the configuration is [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹, not the expected 3d⁴ 4s².

q: The electronic configuration of copper (Z = 29) is:
x: Copper is an exception: a completely filled 3d¹⁰ is extra stable, so it is [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹ rather than 3d⁹ 4s². 3d¹⁰ 4s² would need 30 electrons (zinc).

q: The electronic configuration of the Fe²⁺ ion (Fe, Z = 26) is:
x: Fe is [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s². When it forms an ion, the 4s electrons are removed first, so Fe²⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁶. [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s² is the neutral atom.

q: The electronic configuration of the chloride ion, Cl⁻ (Cl, Z = 17), is:
x: Cl⁻ has 17 + 1 = 18 electrons, the same configuration as argon: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶. 3p⁵ is the neutral chlorine atom.

q: The number of unpaired electrons in a nickel atom (Z = 28, [Ar] 3d⁸ 4s²) is:
x: In 3d⁸, the five d orbitals take one electron each and three of them get a second electron, leaving two unpaired. The 4s² pair is fully paired.

q: An element has the electronic configuration [Ne] 3s² 3p⁴. The element is:
x: [Ne] has 10 electrons, plus 6 more gives 16, which is sulphur. Oxygen has the same outer pattern (s² p⁴) but in the second shell: [He] 2s² 2p⁴.

q: The number of unpaired electrons in the Fe³⁺ ion (Fe, Z = 26) is:
x: Fe is [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s². Removing two 4s electrons and one 3d electron gives Fe³⁺ = [Ar] 3d⁵, with one electron in each d orbital: 5 unpaired. Fe²⁺ (3d⁶) has 4.

q: Which ion has the same electronic configuration as neon (Z = 10)?
x: Mg (Z = 12) loses two electrons to leave 10, the configuration 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ of neon. K⁺, Ca²⁺ and Cl⁻ each have 18 electrons, like argon.

q: In potassium (Z = 19), the nineteenth electron enters the:
x: After 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ (18 electrons), the next lowest-energy subshell is 4s (n + l = 4), not 3d (n + l = 5). So K is [Ar] 4s¹.

q: Chromium has the configuration 3d⁵ 4s¹ instead of 3d⁴ 4s² because:
o: 4s has a higher energy than 3d in all atoms
A d subshell cannot hold four electrons
A half-filled d subshell is extra stable
Chromium has an odd atomic number
x: A half-filled (d⁵) or completely filled (d¹⁰) subshell has extra stability, so one 4s electron moves into 3d. Chromium's atomic number, 24, is even.
